utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: While the witness is coming in, I should mention that we were delayed in starting because of a technical problem which has now been remedied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'd remind you the affirmation you made to tell the truth still replies, and Mr. Stamp is finishing his questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Keric.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Last night I was reflecting on some of your answers yesterday, and I noticed that on a couple of occasions you made statements about Obrad Stevanovic, although I did not ask about him at the time. And I'd like to clarify some of these statements you made. You did tell us that you don't know about the segregation of activities or tasks that was made at the top of the MUP; however, you said that Mr. Stevanovic was directly accountable to the minister of interior. And this wasn't in relation to a question which I asked you, but you volunteered that. Can I ask, did you attend the collegium meetings, the ministers' collegium meetings?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, if I may, I'd would just like to say what I meant when I mentioned Mr. Stevanovic with regard to the questions yesterday. Obrad Stevanovic was mentioned in the context of documents, or rather, dispatches which were sent to the secretariats by the ministry and in the context of PJPs which were run, actually, because he was the commander of PJPs of the police of Serbia. Obrad Stevanovic was also as a commander in the rank of the assistant minister of the interior of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I understand what you are saying and to some degree you are repeat what you said yesterday. I just want you to focus on my questions just for now. We'll get to the explanations. Did you attend meetings of the ministers' collegium?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. I did attend collegium meetings once a year. That was standard practice that heads of SUPs or secretariats of the Interior, which were territorial units, to participate at the beginning of every year at working meetings held at the Ministry of the Interior --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When was the last one you attended before you left for the federal ministry?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the last meeting I attended was held at the beginning of 1998. I think it was in the first quarter of that year because that was standard practice for these meetings to take place in the first quarter every year. During --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. You've answered that. The minister also had meetings with his assistant ministers. Did you attend any of those with the six assistant ministers present?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule, on such meetings you always had minister and his associate and he was in charge of these working meetings. I didn't attend these meetings many times. I perhaps attended several such meetings during my entire career.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm speaking specifically about meetings that the minister had with his assistant ministers. Did you attend any of them and when?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've never attended any such meetings. That's the so-called narrow core collegium at the level of the minister and no heads of SUP attended such meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And do you know how often and when Mr. Stevanovic was in Kosovo in 1998?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't know that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and I don't know how many times he came to Kosovo in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How about 1999? Do you know how often he was there in 1999?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about that because I was appointed to the federal ministry after the 1st of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What about before the 1st of May, 1999, do you know how often he was in Kosovo and what he was doing there?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about that. When I was the head of the secretariat in Pristina in the earlier period, he used to come to visit the secretariat but it didn't happen too often, perhaps several times a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I was focussing in the last question on 1999. How about Mr. Djordjevic, the chief of your section, the public security department, do you know what or how often he was in Kosovo in 1998 and what were his role -- what was his role there?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no information about that, and I wouldn't know how many times he came to Kosovo in 1998 nor 1999, in the area of Kosovo and Metohija --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. In that period, do you know what was their respective role, that is, Mr. Djordjevic and Mr. Stevanovic, in respect to PJP operations in Kosovo? Are you in a position to tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With regard to the role of PJPs in Kosovo and Metohija --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, that's not what I asked. Are you able to tell us about Mr. Djordjevic's and Mr. Stevanovic's respective roles in respect to PJP operations in Kosovo in 1999 and 1998?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With regard to the role of Obrad Stevanovic, he was the commander of all PJPs, and I think he had a direct role in assigning, commanding, and other issues regarding the operations of the PJPs. In terms of Mr. Djordjevic as chief of the public security department, I wouldn't know what his role was in Kosovo in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm asking you specifically about his role in respect to the PJPs, and I'm asking about 1998 and 1999. Do you know what, if any, role he had in respect to the PJPs in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, dear Colleague Stamp, he's been asking the same question for the fourth time and last three times the witness has already responded. And I believe that it's not appropriate to ask the same question for the fourth time because he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Carry on, please, Mr. Stamp. The witness's form of answering is the problem, Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, just if you could focus on the question I asked you. Do you know if General Djordjevic had any role in respect to the PJP operations in Kosovo in 1998 and 1999 and what was it?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know what his role was in terms of subordination and -- in the years of 1998 and 1999 and the PJP's operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You also indicated -- again, I noted on reflection when you were discussing the documents, that these documents, that is the documents deploying the special forces, the PJPs, to Kosovo were signed by Mr. Obrad Stevanovic in many cases. That is something you volunteered. Can I just ask you: How many documents did you see in your career or -- withdrawn. I don't want to go over your entire career so I want to put it specifically to 1998 and 1999. How many documents in that period deploying PJP from Serbia proper to Kosovo did you see signed by Mr. Stevanovic?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I've seen any -- any of these cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Another thing I saw in the transcript which I'd just like to clarify, there's an answer in which you were -- you referred to the police administration and the PJP and you said: "... I know for certain that the police administration was subordinated to public security department. The command of the PJP, I think I've already mentioned this, I think this was in a special status. Formally it was within the police administration. However, I think that it was at a higher level and that it had closer ties with the minister rather than with police administration." Firstly, was the police administration subordinate to the chief of the public security section?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was the PJPs and their organisation a part of the police administration?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in a broader sense, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And what you seem to be indicating is that apart from the formal situation the -- it was at the higher level and that it was closer -- it had closer ties with the minister rather than the police administration. When did this situation arise when the PJP command had closer ties with the minister than the police administration?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say literally as far as I can remember that they were tied closer to the minister. At the times when the security situation escalated and at the times of NATO air-strikes as well as at the times when there was some conflicts in the area of Kosovo and Metohija, so these were the situation you refer to as far as I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we just could move on to something else. You indicated that the standard procedure under the -- or within the framework of the law of Serbia was that in the circumstances you found yourself in where bodies were discovered, there ought to have been a report to the investigating judge and the relevant prosecutor who had jurisdiction over cases of that nature, for them to proceed with an investigation. Yet, you obeyed Mr. Djordjevic's command to send somebody to organise the burial of these bodies in a mass grave. Can you explain why you obeyed this command, having regard to what you know the law stated?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A standard procedure prescribed by the law is as you've explained, but according to the principle of subordination we were obliged to respect and comply with orders from the ministry and senior officials in line with orders. If we had not done that, we would have been subject to disciplinary proceedings or we would -- would have been perhaps removed from the ministry or assigned to different positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The -- did the chief of the public security department or sector have the power to do that?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the principle of subordination and as the chief of the public security department, which means that he's head of one of the departments that we had, public security and state security departments, and he was able to do that and there was no alternative solution to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Ver well. Thank you very much, Mr. Keric, for your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Keric.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: I'm Aleksandar Popovic, member of the Defence team of General Vlastimir Djordjevic. Together with me today are Ms. Marie O'Leary and Mr. Dragoljub Djordjevic. I'm going to be putting some questions to you.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: But before we start, I would kindly ask you to bear in mind that the two of us speak the same language and that we might get carried away in our discussion. Therefore I would kindly ask you to wait before you start giving your answer to allow the interpreters to do their part of the job.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I also add, Mr. Popovic, that please keep short questions or else you will need to slow down considerably because your speech is very quick. So short questions will overcome that.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll bear that in mind. My questions are indeed going to be short, and my introductory remark, however, was rather fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Keric, as I was reading your curriculum vitae I saw that during the period between 1994 and 1997 you were the head of the SUP in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: So I will start with that part, and I will ask you about the security situation in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija -- rather, in Pristina at the time, and in order for me to be more precise, were there any pressures put on the Serbian population during that period or did the Serbian population move out in large numbers from the KiM territory?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the period between 1994 -- or rather, the 1st of June, 1994, and 23rd June, 1997, the security situation in Pristina was changeable, as it were. During that period, there were lots of acts, terrorist acts, explosions, arson, buildings were destroyed and blown up. From time to time there were also ad hoc and organised destructions of public law and order. All that resulted in the emigration of the non-Albanian population from the region of Kosovo and Metohija and Pristina, particularly the Serbs were moving out in large numbers. So the situation was very volatile.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question is this: Am I right in saying that during the period while you were in Kosovo members of the Albanian ethnic group participated in the work of the state organs and organisations, not only as staffers, but also as high-ranking officials in leadership positions?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were such cases, but not on a large scale. As far as I can remember and as far as I followed the situation, sometime in 1990 or 1991 most of the Albanians left state institutions, including the Ministry of the Interior and others. So in this period in question while I was head, there were some sporadic cases or individual cases that they were either high officials in the Ministry of the Interior or the secretariat in Pristina and other state organs in -- the Ministry for Transport and other sectors and departments but their numbers were never large at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Keric. And now my next question refers to the events in the 1990s about which we have heard from several witnesses who have testified before this Trial Chamber. I would like to take you back to the alleged poisoning of Albanian students in the 1990s in the territory of Kosovo. First of all, my question is this: Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that situation. The poisoning of students in primary and other schools started as a mono-national poisoning, that's how it looked like at the time, and this started in the territory of Podujevo municipality. Only a few hours later it spread over the entire territory of Kosovo and Metohija. In my mind, a scenario had been drafted which should have served as the basis for large-scale protests and demonstrations. If you tell somebody that an act of poisoning of children, students, was premeditated, then this is a major foundation and basis and an introduction to other protests, unrests, and possibly a conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Keric. And let me conclude, am I right in saying that all the adequate measures were undertaken at the time and that in that particular case it wasn't established that Albanian pupils had indeed been poisoned. It was actually a propaganda act as you called it and the goal of that propaganda act was to stir large-scale protests of Albanians in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reports prepared by medical teams who examined the allegedly poisoned students were negative; in other words, no poisoning had taken place during that period, which shows that some -- something else was an underlying cause of all that. There was another objective behind that action.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Keric, you were the head of the Uzice SUP between June 1997 and 1st of May, 1999. The first question I have about that stint has to do with the NATO air-strikes. We're starting with the 23rd of March and until the 1st of May, 1999, when you left that position. Could you please tell us what locations in the territory of your secretariat were bombed. And in respect of the time-period, I would kindly ask you to say something specific about Cikota, post in Uzice, and the civilians victims and casualties that were inflicted at the time?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between June 1997 and the 1st of May, 1999, while I was the head of the secretariat in Uzice, to be more precise from the month of March when the campaign started until the 1st of May, the area that was bombed and the targets were military targets in the area of the Uzice secretariat, or rather, the Uzice district. The Ponikve Airport was shelled every day on several occasions every day. It was a military airport. The radio relay facilities were bombed as well as the observation posts of the military. And in addition to the military facilities, there was also collateral damage to certain civilian facilities. For example, the main post office in Uzice was bombed and was razed to the ground as a result, and the civilian facility in Cikota was also bombed. You asked me about that. There were also some human casualties there. I believe that three individuals who had been performing certain duties in that facilities -- facility were killed. And the facility belonged to the medical centre of Cikota, the department for the treatment of the thyroid gland. That was one of the big such institutions in the territory of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Keric, the shelling of the post office in Uzice or Cikota, were those extraordinary events in the Uzice secretariat?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the beginning of NATO campaigns, the state of war was proclaimed and all the events during that period were treated as extraordinary events which were taken place under the state of war because the country was in the state of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did these events have to be reported to the ministry or the sector of public security in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any such case, we informed them about the material damage, human casualties. We sent the ministry Telex messages from reserve locations because the facilities of the ministry had been relocated to some improvised locations because there was an imminent danger that the main building of the secretariat would be shelled, and it did happen on several occasions actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Keric, am I right in saying that so far you have provided several statements about the things you testified about yesterday and today, the first one was to the Working Group on the 27th of January -- 27th of July, 2001, and then on the 8th of June, 2005, in Belgrade to the investigating judge Mr. Dilparic.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true I provided those statements upon a request issued by officials organs and institutions, the Ministry of the Interior, and the special court for war crimes in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday at the beginning of your testimony you told us that due to the lapse of time you will only tell us those things that you remember. Am I right in thinking that in 2001 and 2005 your memory might have been better and you remembered some things better than you do today, nearly ten years or even ten years after the events in question?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is only understandable that some events fade with the passage of time and that I can't really reconstruct all of them properly, as I was able to when it was closer to the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at Exhibit P66.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Keric, we have the document before us. This is the Law on Internal Affairs. What I would be interested in at the moment is Article 7 of the law. We will look at it very briefly. I'm going to read. "The Minister shall determine the manner in which the Ministry of the Interior performs its duties and issues instructions for their performance." Am I right in saying that this is the principle governing the work of the Ministry of the Interior and that that was indeed the role of the minister in it?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minister was the number one person when it came to decrees, instructions, the passing of laws. There's no ambiguity here at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Keric, am I right in saying that when it comes to the event involving dead bodies that you have spoken about, that you were informed about that by the head of the MUP in Bajina Basta and that you informed General Vlastimir Djordjevic by direct telephone line?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in answer to the Prosecutor's question, I explained that that was indeed the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: When you spoke with General Djordjevic, he was in Belgrade, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that he was in Belgrade. I called him by direct telephone line in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And this was not just about that one conversation but all the conversations that you had with him, and you said that there was several such conversations?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were several such conversations because the circumstances imposed the need for us to speak more frequently, and we spoke every time by way of a direct telephone line in the ministry in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that when you spoke to General Djordjevic and told him what you had received about -- as information about the dead bodies in Perucac Lake, General Djordjevic was taken by surprise?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by the tone of his voice, he was obviously taken by surprise, and his comment was something along these lines: This is really not good. What happened is really not good. That's the way I understood him. He was very unpleasantly surprised I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that your impression was that it was a piece of news for him as well?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't confirm, but I can say that his reaction was somewhat unusual. The event itself provoked certain uncertainties amongst us who were on the ground and who had responsibility for the territory because nothing of the kind had happened before. And for me, that was also something unusual, something that was posing an additional burden and it was an unpleasant event, both professionally and in any other term.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Keric, am I right in saying that during the conversation, General Djordjevic never issued an order to you as to what to do? He always said, I'll get back to you later?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't say that he didn't know what to do. On several occasions when I informed him about the event -- to be more specific, the first time when I asked him whether I should inform the prosecutor and others, he told me that he would get back to me a bit later and he did, maybe an hour later, and this repeated on several occasions two or three times during the day that I had to wait for answers about the way I should proceed. I was waiting for the answers from Djordjevic who was in Belgrade, and such answers arrived maybe half an hour to an hour after the initial or original conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: In reference to that, am I right in saying that just like you were duty-bound to report on that incident to your immediate superior, General Djordjevic, he was also in his turn duty-bound to inform his immediate superior, the minister, about such an incident?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that. The logic of the matter following the principle of subordination would speak in favour of that. In this specific case, his superior was the minister. I don't know whether he reported about the event to the minister or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Keric, am I right in saying that during your first conversation General Djordjevic told you that at that particular moment you should not call the investigating judge or prosecutor because the chief of the department for crime prevention had to go to the crime scene to see what had actually happened there?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained that yesterday in answering the prosecutor's question he told me that the chief of the department of -- for crime prevention, Mr. Dimitrijevic [as interpreted], Zoran, should go to the crime scene to secure it to see what the event was all about. And after that when we spoke again we would receive instructions about the possible reporting to the prosecutor or the investigating judge as the persons who have jurisdiction to launch some other investigative actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can we look at P200.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And while we wait for it, Your Honours, I think that there might be an error in the transcript at 16, 6, unless this is a new person we are being told about, that is page 16, line 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can clarify this.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Keric, in the transcript to my question you said who the chief of crime prevention police was. Can you repeat his name.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time when the bodies turned up in Perucac Lake, the head of the crime prevention police department was Major Zoran Mitricevic who is currently head of the police administration in Uzice.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that we have clarified this problem. Let us go back to Exhibit P200. This is a decree on implementing the Law on Criminal Procedure during the state of war. I'm going to ask the Court to produce Article 6 in that decree. Mr. Keric, this decree was in force during NATO air-strikes, or rather, after the state of war was declared. Could you please look at Article 6, bullet point 3 thereof. It says here: "The organ of the interior may in urgent cases carry out investigative activities even without a decision of the public or state prosecutor ..."

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And what's your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Am I right that at that point in time this was a valid provision?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am -- I was not familiar with this decree at the time, and as far as the specific case is concerned, I would say that probably at the moment when we learned about the bodies, but we did not know where they originated from, on whose orders they had been transported and placed there, and why, what was the reason or motive for something like that. Most probably we never looked at that article at the time. If we had known that this was a result of an air-strike or -- and another action, then we would have undertaken specific measures applicable to such conditions as provided for by this article.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, am I also right in saying that this had in total General Djordjevic to order you to first send Mitricevic -- or rather, he didn't know what the person's name was. He referred to him by his position, to check what that was all about?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a legal provision. There's no comment that I can provide. You can see the provision yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Keric, am I right in saying that you didn't tell General Djordjevic that the bodies were civilians because you yourself did not have such information at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I told him that the bodies were of unknown persons and unknown religious and ethnic affiliation, that the bodies were in advanced stages of putrification and decomposition, and that there were no particular markings to show us where the bodies originated from. That's the information that I conveyed to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we then conclude that there was no indicia to tell you that those were bodies of Albanians?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the moment there was no indicia to tell us that the bodies belonged to persons of Albanian ethnic origin. Moreover, initially I had my doubts, which I also said in response to the Prosecutor's question, and I thought that the bodies had been excavated from a mass grave in Bosnia and Herzegovina where the war operations had been taking place as you may well know. At that moment, we didn't know anything about the bodies or the vehicle in which they had been transported there. The first indication about the bodies being the bodies of Albanians was something that I learned from the mass media, from "Vecernje Novosti," the newspaper with the highest circulation, and that was in July 1995 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: The year that we have in the transcript, I believe that you said 2001.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Either I misspoke or the interpreter misinterpreted, but the year was 2001. The year 2001 is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right in saying that you carried out all the orders, bearing in mind that the air-strikes were underway, the state of war was in place. There was a lot of emigration. You had to save people from various adverse events, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, since we didn't know where the bodies had come from, on whose order, and with what intent, I did not dwell upon the problem during those two days because, as I've already explained, the entire areas and facilities in our territory came under air-strikes and we had other priorities which was salvage operations of materiel and humans, that was the first reason; and the second reason was that I was getting ready for my move to the Federal Ministry of the Interior. So during those two days I never went to the lake, and I did not get involved in any concrete activities. I thought that the chief of the crime prevention department would do that because such cases of foul play and this as a result of those were under his jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at P357 and the page number is D002-0364.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Keric, while we're waiting for the document, let me tell you that this is the regulation of the internal organisation of the MUP. I'm interested in Article 6. Can you read from the screen? You don't have to read aloud. I'm just inquiring.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: My question is this: Am I right in saying the PJPs, in keeping with this regulation, are established by the minister?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to this issue, I have already stated my opinion partly in response to the Prosecutor's question. I said that the PJPs were closely tied to the minister of the interior, and when it -- when I say the "PJPs," in addition to the ones that we referred to yesterday and today, I also imply a Special Anti-terrorist Unit and units for special operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Keric, you have been a police officer for a long time. You have held some very responsible duties. My question is this: Do you remember that there were also Special Police units?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We've been discussing that for two days now. Special Police units did exist and their command was at the level of the Ministry of the Interior, as I've already explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see the Exhibit P58.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Keric, this is a decision on the training or education of Special Police units. Am I right in saying that on the basis of Article 6 of the rules on the internal organisation, the article which we saw in the previous document, the minister of the interior is responsible for training?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear. There is no need to comment that.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you read under paragraph 2, under point 2, sub-point 2.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The tasks and duties" --

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: No, that's the first one, the next one, please.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The third one?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: No. It says number 3. "Professional education, training, and maintenance" -- sorry, "bringing into readiness, mobilising, and engaging the PJMs on performing tasks defined in paragraph 1 of this item shall be done upon the orders of the minister and when approved by the minister also upon the orders of the chief of the public security department." I believe I tried to explain that in response to the Prosecutor's questions during yesterday's sessions when I said that the PJPs and the commander who had the status of an assistant minister were more closely tied to the minister when it came to equipment, training, and all other PJP units' issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: So -- so we're not talking here about closer ties or not -- but we're saying that bringing into readiness, mobilising, and engaging was something that was ordered only by the minister or by somebody who had the approval of the minister?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is in the decision. If it's there then that's correct. I was not part of the top management of the ministry and I couldn't say who had which powers at that time. It's in the decision, and from the decision it's very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Keric, am I right in saying that Special Police units, PJPs, were formed for the territory of the entire Serbia and not only for the purpose of the area of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These units were set up for the entire area of Serbia, and they were structured as detachments. To be more specific, the 35th Detachment had Special Police units of the secretariats, Valjevo, Kraljevo, Sabac, Novi Pazar, Cacak, and Uzice.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right in saying that these units were used in regular and extraordinary circumstances in the entire territory of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were used when needed in the entire territory of the Republic of Serbia. Most often, it was in the area of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that these units were used to prevent and suppress demonstrations and unrests in the territory of the entire Serbia, most often in the city of Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In -- during regular security situations, these units were used to maintain public order and peace when some mass events took place. They were also used to prevent demonstrations. And during the state of war, they had special powers. But at that time I was not part of the ministry, and I couldn't comment on that, especially with regard to the year 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see Exhibit P257.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Before that, I apologise, I have a suggestion or a comment. On page 21, line 1 and 2, instead of "under authorities" it says "after the decision." So I will repeat my question. Mr. Keric, as we said, the deployment of special units and establishment, was that something that was only done under the orders of the minister and somebody authorised by the minister?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Bringing into readiness, establishment, and deployment was done in accordance with the orders of the Special Police commander. It was usually the head of the public security department, I suppose. And I also think since the establishment was something under the authorities of the minister upon the proposal of the commander, it was also verified by the minister. These are people who were able to bring forces into readiness and deployment of units to be assigned.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Let's not assume. Let us take a look at the decision on the formation of the 124th Intervention Brigade of the PJPs or Special Police units. You can see again that on the basis of Article 6 of the rules on internal organisation, this decision was made. Can you again look at Article 2, paragraph 2. The sentence begins with: "Putting the intervention brigade on standby ..."

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says undoubtedly that: "Putting the intervention brigade on standby, assembly, and engagement for the tasks in paragraph 1 shall be done upon the orders of the minister ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right in thinking that members of the intervention brigade formed duties when they were not engaged in PJPs?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All police officers, policemen, performed their regular policing duties until the moment when they issued an order that they should be mobilised and deployed in the performance of an extraordinary task.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right in thinking that once a unit was deployed - and I'm talking about a PJP - you did not receive any reports about the units' activities?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: PJPs and their activities were beyond our jurisdiction and control. Therefore, we were not in a position to receive any reports about their activities, about their engagement, about the interventions that they were involved in. We only received information and reports if some of the unit members from the territory of our secretariat were wounded, injured, or killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right in saying that you reported to the police administration and the command of PJPs only about members of PJPs who were deployed or if somebody did not go to the field and why?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already provided an answer to that question yesterday. I and chiefs of regional secretariats or most often chiefs of police departments used their professional line to send the reports to the commands of PJPs or the public security sector about the number of people who were engaged, the way they were transported, and the directions of their movement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, before we lose it off the screen, page 23, line 9 to 11, the transcript has recorded only part of the paragraph 1 which is on the screen -- paragraph 2 which is on the screen before us. The witness referred to it as the minister being authorised, but the paragraph goes on to say: "... and on his authorisation of the chief of the public security department." I think that omission should be noted before we lose it off the screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, Your Honour. I shall therefore repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to kindly ask you, sir, to read under Article 2, paragraph 2, which begins with the words: "Putting the intervention brigade on standby ..." My question to you was: Who was it who was authorised to put on standby, assembly, and engage members of the Special Police unit?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In one of your previous questions or in answer to one of your previous questions I've already explained that because the same provision is contained in the decree on the establishment of such police units. The text is the same: "Putting the intervention brigade on standby, assembly, and engagement ..." And intervention brigade is just one of the units. It is not in the broader sense of that term within the framework of PJPs as far as I understand. And I continue: "... assembly and engagement for the tasks in paragraph 1 of this item shall be done on the orders of the minister and, on his authorisation, of the chief of the public security department."

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the Court please produce P01184.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Keric, this is a dispatch that you had an occasion to see yesterday. My question is this: Is this a normal dispatch of the kind that you received and saw during your work?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a standard dispatch dealing with the preparation and informing people who belonged to PJPs about sending them on a mission, informing them about the time that -- when they would be sent on that mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that the dispatch also concerns your own Secretariat of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does concern my secretariat because it says the engagement of members -- or rather, it says that the engagement is hereby finished and that they will be replaced by other detachments and other secretariats.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And now, could you please look at that third paragraph in this document. It starts with the following words: "The members of the PJP are to be dispatched in their intervention uniforms for urban conditions with joint weapons ... with short-barrelled and long-barrelled guns ..." My question to you, sir, is this: Am I right in saying that the weapons in question are weapons that members of a PJP are issued with in their own unit?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, this is the establishment weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's my question.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The establishment weapons that they are issued with for their policing duties normally and with all the particular weaponry that is listed here and pieces of equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: You've already spoken about this, but let me put it this way: Am I right in saying that the police administration provided only logistical support to PJPs?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the police administration at the ministry level is concerned, I don't know whether they only provided logistical support; and when it comes to the police department as the organisational unit within the Secretariats of the Interior, the organisational unit of the police administration, they only -- they did not even provide logistical support. They were only in charge of informing men about the mission, the time, and the mode of transportation. Everything else is within the jurisdiction of the command of PJPs.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: I'll take the opportunity, Mr. Keric, to ask you something else. Am I right in saying that you were not in command of PJPs once they were sent out to Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the structure of the duties that I performed from the very beginning until the moment I was retired, I was never in command of PJPs, nor did I have such authorities ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Court please produce the second page of this same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Keric, we've already discussed this -- or rather, you already spoke or started commenting upon this document yesterday. And the issue here is that the dispatch was not signed. Am I right in saying that a document which is not signed in this particular form could not be sent by the normal communication means? What I'm saying is that the chief of communications would not have accepted an unsigned document for sending?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the person best suited to answer your question is the chief of communications administration or the person in charge of communications. In my opinion, he could not send a document that was not signed in somebody's own handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now could the Court please produce P346.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Keric, this is another dispatch, and this was shown to you yesterday. The number it bears is 587. My question to you is this: Is this a customary dispatch?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by the style of writing, the heading, the text, this is a standard form of dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that in this dispatch there is no reference to any anti-terrorist activities?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on page 1. I can't see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at page 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The term "terrorism" is not mentioned on page 2 as far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that this dispatch actually deals with securing meals and payment of per diem; the regular duties and relief of people from regular duties; the equipment that should be given to them when they're sent on a mission; how long they would stay? In other words, there is no single reference to any combat activities or anti-terrorist activities?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular case, the issues discussed here fall within the purview of logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would kindly ask the Court to produce P01195 which has been marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Keric, this is yet another dispatch that was shown to you yesterday and is the answer to dispatch number 587 dated 21st March, 1999, the one that we have just had an occasion to see. First of all, am I right in saying that this dispatch was sent by the chief of department -- rather, then the chief of the secretariat?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already answered that in response to the Prosecutor's question, and it says unambiguously that the dispatch was signed by the chief of the police department and not the chief of the Kikinda Secretariat. And the dispatch was sent to the command of the PJPs with the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Does that fact also illustrate that those were the most customary and regular activities, the most normal type of reports that were sent at the time?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I've already said that. This is just a regular report. Reports of this kind could have been sent by the police department because the tasks described therein fall within the purview of the police administration and PJPs, and they could also be sent by the chief of the secretariat, which was the most common case as we have already seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the Court please produce P01201.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Keric, this dispatch was shown to you yesterday as well. My question primarily refers to this. Am I right in saying that everything that is contained herein falls within the scope of regular policing activities? And if -- we can also show you the second page, should you wish us to do so.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I see it, this dispatch refers to the time when the security measures were stepped up. There were some calculations with sending people out on missions. And there was an increased number of sick-leave days and absence without permission. And I believe that the whole dispatch is the result of that. I'm not very clear on what it says. In any case, this was in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: My next question is this: Am I right that this was sent to all the secretariats in the entire territory in the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all the secretariats which you can see in the heading.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that we have come to the break time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We must have our first break now. We resume at 3.30. The Court Officer will assist you in the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Keric, I apologise for a digression, but let's go back to the beginning of my questioning today. I would like to know, with regard to the poisoning case or the alleged poisoning of Albanian students that we talked about, were you in the territory of Kosovo at that time; and if you had been there, what was your function?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time of the poisoning event, I was in Pristina. I don't have my legal decision with me, but I spent about 40 days in Pristina. And during that time-period the poisoning case happened, the alleged poisoning, in primary schools. First it was primary schools but other schools as well later. I was the coordinator for security affairs, if we may call it that way, in the security centre in Pristina involving several municipalities of the Pristina region, municipalities included were Lipljan, Glogovac, Podujevo, Kosovo Polje. I may have missed out some municipalities. So that's the area we covered from the secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My question was about your direct involvement or direct information you received since you were in the area.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that period the head of the security centre was Hajid Bujoki [phoen], he was an Albanian, and he coordinated all activities in the territory of Pristina and especially the activities regarding the poisoning event.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's now see Exhibit P01203 MFI.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Keric, another exhibit which was shown to you yesterday during the afternoon session, it may seem to you as a repetition, but I have some questions with regard to that document. Am I right in saying that this dispatch was sent to all secretariats in the territory of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was sent to all secretariats.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that a dispatch of this type, we can see that this is a dispatch ordering update of plans and so on. Is this kind of dispatch in line with the Defence Act, and I think you are well positioned to say that.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The mobilisation plan as terminology relates more to the military organisation. In extraordinary circumstances, it also relates to the MUP organisation, especially when it comes to mobilisation of Special Police units and the active staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. However, can you tell us from the way the dispatch was written, is this concerned with regular police activities of the public security department?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Keric.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I see P1205 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Keric, this is a dispatch from the 15th of January, 1999. And my question again is this: Is this a dispatch for the entire territory of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the entire territory of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the first sentence. You don't have to read it out. That's the sentence beginning with: "The government ..." So my question with regard to that sentence is this: Am I right in saying that the basis for sending this dispatch are the relevant decisions of the Government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Government of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Keric --

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the second page of this dispatch, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday some questions were put forward to you with regard to what it says on the second page. Can you please read the paragraph, the first paragraph, on this page. And I will have some questions about it after you've read it.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: This is my question: Am I right in saying that in this dispatch they're talking about regional secretariats, covering travel routes, and check-points toward the province of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This dispatch is about regional secretariats which are close to the Kosovo and Metohija province, but at the same time, this dispatch was sent as a mandatory dispatch to the secretariats in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija in terms of stepped-up checks of travellers, luggage, and vehicles, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: I agree. But in the sentence it says that: "... it's therefore necessary for the regional secretariats covering the travel routes and check-points towards the AP KiM and Republic of Montenegro step up their efforts ..."

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said this is intended to the secretariats, regional secretariats, which are close to the Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The last part says: "The MUP of the Republic of Serbia ... will visit check-points and regional secretariats in order to verify whether the ordered measures are being implemented in their entirety." Am I right in saying that regional secretariats covering travel routes and checking points toward AP KiM will be covered? So this is in fact the control exercised over something which was suggested in the previous paragraph?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the control exercised by the ministry, according to what I can see, and by the secretariat, so both the ministry and the secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, were check-points something that existed in the entirety territory of Serbia? Were check-points present in the most important routes throughout Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no reason to have them. In this specific case, there were some specific measures for the Kosovo and Metohija province. And this dispatch is about -- about those parts of Serbia which are close to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: So this is towards not in the territory of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: That's important to say. I have another question about this dispatch or several ones. Can we be more precise and say that these are local secretariats, not regional, because it's not the same when you have regional and local secretariats?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we're talking about local secretariats. Maybe that's better terminology.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we can please go back to the first page of this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Keric, in the heading we can see that this dispatch dated January 15th, 1999, was sent - and am I right in saying that - that this was sent on the date of January the 15th, 1999?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's -- I suppose that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It says "Belgrade" below. Am I right in saying that that was sent from Belgrade on January the 15th?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, according to the date that's not an issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Keric.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see Exhibit D258.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Keric, am I right in saying that this dispatch was sent to all Secretariats of the Interior in the territory of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us who sent the dispatch?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was sent by the chief of administration, Major-General Slobodan Spasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, is this dispatch a regular type of activity? So does it talk about regular types of police activities?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This dispatch was sent by the chief of administration of the fire-fighting department or the fire protection police sections, and it is related to fire protection measures if I see well from the dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: So these are regular police activities?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see Exhibit D255.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Keric, was this dispatch also sent to all secretariats in the territory of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us who sent the dispatch?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was sent by the chief of administration, Major-General Dragan Ilic. He was head of the crime police department within the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that this dispatch also describes regular police activities?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please produce Exhibit D262.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Keric, was this dispatch also sent to all secretariats in the territory of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please turn to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us who sent the dispatch.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Assistant Minister, Major-General Petar Zekovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Does this dispatch also talk about regular police activities?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it covers the area for which the general was in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see Exhibit D261.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Keric, was this dispatch sent to all secretariats in the territory of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go to page 2 of the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us who sent the dispatch.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was sent by the assistant minister, Major-General Stojan Misic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Does this dispatch also describe common and regular police activities?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's part of the jurisdiction or remit of this assistant minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the Court Officer to put up Exhibit D04285. I will repeat the number. The number is D004-2859. Thank you. That's the document I was looking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Keric, these are minutes from the county court or district court in Belgrade, war crime chambers, Investigative Judge Dilparic, and it's minutes of a conversation with you, Mr. Keric. Do you remember that this interview happened on the 8th of June, 2005, in front of this judge?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I gave the statement in 2003 if we're talking about the exact year. It may have happened later. That was my second statement I gave after the statement given to the Working Group of the MUP in Belgrade in 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. Mr. Keric, do you remember that the investigative judge of the district court in Belgrade asked questions and that during your statement you talked about the same issues you talked about here today?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that these questions covered the same topic and I think that most of the questions were related with the same case.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Keric, am I right in saying that -- considering we said that was 2005, am I right in saying that back then you were able to remember some things better than today since four years have passed since then?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was 2003 - I may be wrong - but of course it's understandable that after the passage of time some memories can be -- can fade.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I suggest this exhibit to be confirmed or accepted -- admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there any particular passage to which you draw attention?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the full statement to be tendered into evidence because the witness talked about the same issues which were discussed today and yesterday. There are some parts which are of minor or major relevance, but the entire statement is a logical part, logical statement, which was given back then to the investigating judge in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the witness seems to be questioning the date. And the date of this document is in 2005. So I think the witness has to be asked questions about the contents for him to verify whether or not this is his statement and to explain whatever answers he might have given insofar as the relevance of the issues in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: My concern was to know which parts of this document were thought to be material to the account that he has given in evidence here. If you are relying on particular differences, they should be drawn to his attention and his comment obtained.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. Could we turn to page 5, paragraph 1, in B/C/S. I would assume that it is the same also.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Keric, kindly look at the sentence starting with: "At some time ..." That's the seventh line of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please read this sentence to us.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "For some time Zoran Mitricevic and I consulted about what to do and he suggested that they be recovered and buried. The burial should take place in the vicinity of Perucac dam. This is what Zoran suggested and I believe at that time we did not have any other option. Since the number of bodies went up I believe that we should not inform either the investigating judge or anybody else. I informed Mr. Krivokapic, the investigating judge, I believe that his name was Momcilo or Momo in Uzice, I informed him about the event and I don't know whether they came to the scene of the crime because I did not get involved after that."

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Keric, in this sentence it says that you and Zoran consulted as to what to do and you agreed, you and Zoran Mitricevic. You decided to take the bodies out of the water and bury them. So this was an agreement between you and Mitricevic. You're not talking about the chief of the public security sector and his order?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this is a mistake in the interpretation. I can't be sure. In any case, the fact is that we could not do anything without the orders and consultations as I described them yesterday. Whether there came a time when we were discussing dilemma as to what to do -- because for a long time we were not aware of the position of the head of the sector. I believe it is possible that there had been conversations to that effect. In any case, the burial only took place after the order of the chief of the sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now go to page 7, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The English page was not on the screen about that passage. Do you know which it is for our purposes?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we received the English translation very late and that is why we did not manage to find the corresponding references for what I am reading from in the B/C/S version. I believe that it won't be a problem locating that. Can we go to page 6 in the English version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The last passage that this was referring to is in the bottom of page 3 in the English, the last two lines of page 3 and the first full paragraph of page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the last sentence which continues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now you were turning to another paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] yes, please. Page 7 in B/C/S, paragraph 2. Could we also display the English version. I believe that the text is on page 6, page 6 -- page 6 is the corresponding page. Or perhaps page 5 in the English version. Maybe you should try that.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you can now look at the page. Mr. Keric, on page 7 the investigating judge puts a question to you. "Let's go back to the chief of sector, did he provide you with any instructions or not?" And your answer is this: "He did not provide us with any instructions."

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't hear your question. I did not hear your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Is it better now?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, now it's better.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Page 7, and I'm reading, the investigating judge is putting a question to you. "Let's go back to the chief of sector. Did he provide you with any instructions or not?"

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't hear you. I believe that we have a technical error. I can't hear your question. Now I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, now I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: The investigating judge asks you: "Let's go back to the chief of the department. Did he or didn't he give you any instructions?" Or not -- hold on. I have not put my question.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Your answer: "He did not give any instructions. We had no other way out but to act." The next question on the part of the investigating judge: "Then tell me, who decided to have the bodies recovered from the water and buried?" Your answer: "We decided. We consulted Zoran. We asked him what to do. He suggested that they be recovered and buried. I agreed with that. We had no other option, Your Honour. At the time we could not do anything else." Mr. Keric, quite contrary to what you told us yesterday, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Firstly, he should inquire of the witness whether or not this is his recollection of what was asked and what was said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Carry on, please, Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Keric, this is quite contrary to what you stated yesterday?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I stated yesterday is correct. I don't remember this interpretation, although this interpretation was valid for a while until we had a confirmation of the chief of department about how to deal with the bodies. And the final position was for the bodies to be recovered and buried in the soil in the vicinity of Perucac dam.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: However, Mr. Keric, the question was: "Then tell me, who decided to have the bodies recovered from the water and buried?" Your decisive answer was this: "We decided." You didn't say "the chief of department." You said: "We decided. We consulted Zoran, asked him what to do. He suggested that they be recovered and buried. I agreed with that ..." Absolutely nowhere is there a reference to the "chief of department."

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a preliminary conversation pending the final decision of the chief of department.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Keric, did the investigating judge warn you at the beginning of your statement that you were duty-bound to tell the truth?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that, and I took a solemn declaration, just as I did yesterday before this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Did he also warn you that false testimony is an offence?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this is not a subject of my -- today's testimony, and I would kindly ask the Trial Chamber to take into account what I said yesterday. I adhere by that, and I adhere by the statement that I provided yesterday before this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now turn to page 8 of the same statement. That's also the following page in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: The investigating judge asked you: "Therefore, if I understood you well, you did not have any option that would have come to you from Belgrade. You yourselves decided what to do with the bodies." You answer: "We did not have any solution provided to us." So you are asserting, you're claiming for the third time in this statement that there was no other solution or order from Belgrade on the table. You yourselves decided what to do with the bodies.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already explained that there was no way we could have not carried out the order to recover the bodies and bury them. I already explained that yesterday in answering the Prosecutor's question and today. We didn't know. I didn't know as the chief of the secretariat where the bodies came from, on whose orders, who put them at the dam, and with what intention and goal was this done. In my view, the way I understood things, this violated all the codices, moral, professional, and this was contrary to the provisions of both the international and national laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: This is all good and well, Mr. Keric, but that was not my question. I'm reading for the third time. There was a very clear question put to you by the investigating judge, and you, equally clearly, answer that you did not have any solution that would have been ordered to you from Belgrade and that you yourselves decided what to do with the dead bodies. When did you speak the truth? Are you telling us the truth today or did you tell the truth then?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both then and now. I believe that something was missed from the interpretation of my answers. Without consulting my superiors in the ministry, I could not have undertaken measures to recover and bury the bodies, and -- nor did I have any reason to do so. And these reasons arise from the fact that I've previously explained to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Let's move on to the following paragraph. The investigating

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SAYS
utterances.text: "Tell me, did anybody from Belgrade mention anything, and here I'm primarily thinking of the chief of the department, in connection with those bodies, did he suggest what should be done apart from what you said: That nobody was to be informed about it?" Witness Djordje Keric answers: "There were no suggestions, Your Honour, except when I first contacted the chief of the department to inform him that some bodies had surfaced, that there were floating bodies ..." Mr. Keric, the fourth time you clearly answer a question put to you and you say clearly that there were no suggestions from Belgrade. The very clear question put to you here was whether there were any suggestions on the part of the chief of the department, and you again claim there were no suggestions. Are you still trying to tell me that what you're saying today is absolutely the same to what you were saying then?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember everything in view of the passage of time. I don't remember what I said at the district court. And I repeat, the truth is what I said yesterday and what I'm saying today, before this Trial Chamber. Everything was done in consultation and especially the recovery and the burial of the bodies from Perucac dam. It was all done on the order of the head of the department, Colonel Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
