utterances.text: Mr. Keric, we have still not come to an end of our discussion about the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 13, paragraph 1, in B/C/S, and we will have to try and find the corresponding page in English. Yes, we have the correct English page. Let's look at the penultimate paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Keric, again you're answering the judge's questions and you are saying: "He couldn't have received such an order. I certainly wouldn't have given it nor would I have carried out such an order from the ministry level. Actually, I said that because the chief of the department had no clear stand that the bodies were to be recovered and buried on land until further notice, until the investigation was completed, until it was known what this was all about, where they were from, and who had done this ..." Mr. Keric, this could not have been put any more clearly. And I'm asking you again: What is the truth? This is the fifth time in this statement that you repeat to a very precise question that you personally, you and nobody else, ordered for the bodies to be recovered and buried on land until further notice.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want my answer? I did not have any reason or motive or authority to do so without consulting the chief of the department first. If you look at the Official Note of the Working Group of the Ministry of the Interior dating back to July 2001 when I provided my first statement, then you will see that I said it very clearly there, that I said to the chief of the department that I didn't want to participate in the recovery and the burial of the bodies, primarily because I was not aware of where they came from and under whose orders. I was quite revolted by that act, and at one point I said to the inspectors who had gone there to organise the recovery of the bodies that this defies all the principles of common sense and that whoever did that was no less than a psychiatric case, to put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Keric, I don't doubt it for a second that you were very embittered when you learned about all that; however, my question is this: You were warned by the investigating judge in Belgrade that a false testimony is a criminal offence. And after that you claim in five different places that you were the one who issued the order for the bodies to be recovered and buried. And there is no single place where you make a reference to the head of the public sector department. Moreover, you say very clearly that he did not have anything to do with all that, that you did not receive any instructions from him. And now, four years later, you come here and you are telling us something completely different.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not something completely different. I apologise. The act was committed by somebody. Somebody brought all the bodies to the dam and they did what they did. Everything else was just paraphernalia, the recovery, the burial, and everything else. At that moment when nobody knew where the bodies came from, who had committed the crime, and with what intention. What the inspectors did on the screen, for example, maybe Zoran Mitricevic had consulted his superior, the head of the administration of the crime police of Serbia, Mr. Dragan Ilic, or maybe somebody else. And maybe this was done in order to receive instructions for the bodies to be buried pending the investigation on the origin of the bodies and the perpetrators who committed the crime. That was the main objective in my view, to elucidate the crime. It was not my main point to see who it was who issued the order. And I don't think we should dwell upon the circumstances any longer. I adhere by the statement provided to the Trial Chamber. As to how this interpretation came about and whether there are any dilemmas in this interpretation, Your Honour, I'm really not sure. The essence of the matter is the whole event and not the action of recovery and burial.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Keric. Let's now move on to a different matter that I would like to discuss with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Does this still concern this statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I've still not finished dealing with the statement. I have a couple more questions arising from the statement and then I will tender it into evidence. I believe my reasons will be clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We are now still with the same statement, page 11, paragraph 3, in the B/C/S version. I apologise once again for not knowing the corresponding page in the English version, but I hope ...

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: So when a direct question was put to you by the investigating judge, did you -- were you informed at some point that there is a refrigerator lorry in the lake; your reply was: "No. I was informed that it's a refrigerated lorry only from the mass media later on. I think that I found about it -- found out about it in the newspapers for the first time. Before that, nobody or at least myself didn't know anything about it." Mr. Keric, is there any difference between this and what you said before this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My reply was the response to the question on whether that was the refrigerated truck with the bodies of Albanians which we already talked about. At that point in time, neither myself, Mitricevic, nor the group of inspectors knew that this was a refrigerator truck -- it was actually a container of the truck with bodies of unknown origin. At that point in time we didn't know whether these were of Albanian ethnicity or some other.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender this evidence, and I think I've provided sufficient number of reasons for the admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I just ask that counsel indicate what is the provenance of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an official document from the court in Belgrade, a district court from Belgrade, war crime chambers, investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that apparent on the document anywhere?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You can see that on the first page of the document. In the upper right corner the registration number of the case is given and the heading starts with: "Belgrade District Court, War Crimes Chamber, Investigating Judge Milan Dilparic, in the presence of the recording clerk Katica Lekic ..." and so on and so on, "... proceeding with the questioning of the witness Djordje Keric."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We haven't seen the whole document. Is there at seal or a signature of the judge at the end of the document, or something of that nature?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] this is a reproduction of an audio-tape, and the audio-tape is available at the district court in Belgrade. This is also an official document. And in this document the investigating judge at page 15, which is the last page of the document, states that the interview ended at 10.10. And if there's need, we can deliver also the audio-tape. We can request that from the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is this a typewritten transcript prepared by the court ?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Have you got some covering letter from the court to show that it was sent to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] let me just say that the same transcripts have already been used in this -- in these proceedings, some of them were used when we had witness Veljkovic by Mr. Stamp's, and we have the supporting documentation from the National Council which is in charge for the cooperation with the ICTY. And we can -- we can give you that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp is presently questioning the authenticity of this document. We're told, Mr. Stamp, that you yourself used it in part --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no, I have not used this document --

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say this document. I said this type of document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Counsel will address the Chamber, not each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed. Documents emanating from the district court have been used, but if I was asked by the Chamber where I got it from, I would have said that I got it from the district court, from Mr. Dilparic. I'm just asking where did the Defence get this document from. That is all. I mean, all of these documents, if the Prosecution use them, we can explain and show a trail of evidence where we got them from.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber will, Mr. Popovic, mark this document for identification, pending some verification, covering letter, or something, to indicate its source.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will send you that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be D00316 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I've completed my questioning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, thank you very much for that and for the directness and selection of your questioning. Yes, Mr. Stamp, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I ask you first of all, Mr. Keric, in respect to this statement that you gave to investigating judge Mr. Dilparic on more than one occasion you said that your recollection is that you gave this statement in 2003. Can you recall if you were employed or what were you doing as your occupation at the time you were interviewed by Judge Dilparic.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dear Mr. Prosecutor, I don't remember exactly whether it was 2003 or 2005. I thought originally it was 2003, but Mr. Dilparic will know exactly. On the 1st of July, 2002, I was retired from my position in the Ministry of the Interior, and when I was giving my statement I was a retired person at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. This document I have or has you saying -- and the first part I want to read to you is the first part the Defence read to you. It says that you said: "At one point Zoran Mitricevic consulted also about what to do and where we could start recovering the bodies from the water and putting them, that is, laying them on the ground, burying them near the Perucac dam, which Zoran himself also suggested and I don't think we had any option at that time." Do you recall saying that to Mr. Dilparic?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I do not recall in what context it was said. If it was said, I suppose it was said at the moment of the interview when we still didn't have the clear view of the chief of department. Without the clear view of chief of department, we had no authority to undertake any measures of burial --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: My question was simply whether or not you recall saying to Mr. Dilparic what I just read to you, and I take it from what you are saying is that you don't recall that?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not recall that. I can't recall exactly what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It also is recorded here that you were asked by the investigating judge: "Let's go back to the chief of the department. Did he or didn't he give you any instructions?" This document records you as saying: "He didn't give any instructions. We had no option but to act." Do you recall telling the investigative judge that?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that. I said -- I remember I said we shouldn't do something about the bodies until the final decision is made about the burial.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Further, you were asked about this passage, the document says -- that the investigating judge asked you: "Tell me, did anybody from Belgrade mention anything? And here I am primarily thinking of the chief of department in connection with those bodies. Did he suggest what should be done apart from what you said, that nobody was to be informed about it?" And the document goes on to say that you answered: "There were no suggestions." Do you recall telling Mr. Dilparic that there were no suggestions by Mr. Djordjevic in that regard?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that. I probably said that something like that happened at an initial stage, where we had no clear stand from the chief of department about the burial.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And it says here in this document that the investigating judge asked you: "If I understand correctly, you had no solution ordered by Belgrade but you yourself decided what to do with the bodies" -- I should re-read that last part. "So if I understand you correctly, you had no solution ordered by Belgrade but you yourselves decided what to do with the bodies?" And this is -- you replied: "We had no solution at all." Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall answering that. It may be that we talked about measures that were applied during the first day because the order about the burial happened on the second day after the consultations with the chief of department.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And do you recall telling Mr. Dilparic that no instructions were received from the ministry or from the chief of department of the ministry?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall that. I think that I said we were asking for orders on what to do in terms of the burial of bodies on the land near to the dam site.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. You were asked some questions and in one of your responses you referred to your original statement to the Working Group that interviewed you when this event became a matter of public note. I think it was suggested to you that your memory in 2005, when you were supposed to have given what's written in this document, would have been fresher than it is now. So I would like to allow you to have a look at the document or your statement of 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we bring up document D004-2856, that's the B/C/S; and the English translation is D004-2853. Let's just go to the end of both documents first. While we are there we can see it's your statement of the 27th of January, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's your signature, Mr. Keric?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is a signed statement that you gave in 2001 when this issue broke in the press?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This statement was given in 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we return to the first page of it. Look at the first paragraph, for the record, at the top it was given at the premises of the crime police administration of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is that your memory?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we now turn to page 2 -- or before we move we should probably just read into the record for the English at least. I think we should remain on page 1 in the B/C/S -- no, no, I think we can move to both -- let me read what the bottom of page 1 in the English says. Can we scroll down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: "One day in April 1999 as chief of the secretariat in Uzice I received a telephone call from the chief of the Bajina Basta OUP Captain Slavko" - and if we could move to page 2 because it's Captain Slavko Petrovic. Could we move to the B/C/S corresponding section, please - "he told me that in the area of Perucac Lake near Bajina Basta a number of dead bodies emerged and were floating on the surface. At that moment I suspected, as there was a war on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that these dead bodies were from that area, that they were a consequence of the mopping-up of the terrain. So I ordered Captain Petrovic to hold off taking further action until I personally contacted the MUP officials. "I phoned General Vlastimir Djordjevic the chief of the Public Security Service. I informed him about the event and asked for his opinion on the procedure to be taken, suggesting to him that we inform the representatives of the judicial organs. General Djordjevic told me to send Zoran Mitricevic, the chief of the Uzice SUP to obtain the necessary information and then to inform the General of the situation and not to inform the representatives of the judicial organs ..." Is that what you see in your copy and do you recall making that statement?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall giving such a statement. But just let me correct you. You said that Mr. Mitricevic was the chief of the Uzice SUP. At that time he was the chief of the crime police department in the Uzice SUP, and as ordered by Mr. Djordjevic, he came to the scene after I conferred orders to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I was reading what's in the statement. You said: "Pursuant" -- In the next paragraph. I -- is that on your page? You said: "Pursuant to the order of General Djordjevic, Zoran Mitricevic, and Slavko Petrovic, the chief of the Bajina Basta OUP, were sent to the spot. And then there the above mentioned informed me over the phone that some 20 dead bodies were floating in the water close to the hydro-electric power zone and the left bank from the up-stream direction. Having received information from the spot, I again informed the chief of the service, General Djordjevic and he ordered that measures be taken for the clearing --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down while reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if this is the way to admit the statement without requiring to tender it by means of reading every part of it, I think it's much simpler, in fact, for him to do that; but the fact is that only a few paragraphs are relevant, and I don't think the entire statement should be read. That's my objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't propose to read the entire thing. I just want him to confirm whether or not he said certain things because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You are entitled to have the witness read those parts of the statement you think are either confirmatory of the evidence he's given or deal with parts that you suggest are contrary to what is being put to him by Defence counsel. I haven't yet detected that you're reading unnecessarily against that background, but I'm sure you'll bear that in mind, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm guided, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'll return to where I started on this last passage. "Pursuant to the order of General Vlastimir Djordjevic, Zoran Mitricevic and Slavko Petrovic, the chief of the Bajina Basta OUP, were sent to the spot. There and then the above mentioned informed my over the phone that some dead bodies were floating in the water close to the hydro power-plant zone and the left bank from the upstream direction. Having received the information from the spot, I again informed the chief of the service, General Djordjevic, and he ordered that measures be taken for clearing up the terrain, saying that he will send the representatives of the Republic of Serbia MUP to the spot for coordination of the clearing of the terrain." Do you recall saying that in your statement to the MUP Working Group?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall giving the statement, and we did have that interview. The issue whether somebody did come from the ministry is something to be answered by the crime police department chief because he was there all the time and he was there when the decision was made to make the burial.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In this statement you said that General Djordjevic ordered that measures be taken for the clearing-up of the terrain. Could you explain what you mean or what you meant when you said this in your statement. What does that -- what were you saying here?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I meant was the retrieval of bodies from the dam, from the container, because a number of bodies were kept in the container of the lorry and putting them on the land. So that's what the term covers, retrieval and the preparation of bodies to be buried in line with the orders that came after from the chief of department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise, but there is something in the transcript. It says "asanacija" in the B/C/S version, not clearing-up of the -- and I think there's some difference. But the Serbian version is more credible because the statement was given to the organs in Serbia. Just the word. It says not "clearing-up" but "asanacija "is the word used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you able to tell me your understanding of the word "asanacija"?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My understanding of the word is that that's a word which is used in military terminology and it means clearing-up of the field in an appropriate way, but I think that the word "asanacija" is used in all other languages because I suppose it's not a Serbian word by origin. So it means the removal of bodies, animals, people, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We know the sense in which you understand it. I don't at the moment think that that suggests there's something fundamentally wrong with what is being put to us in this interpretation that is here. You would give it a specific context of a military cleaning up, perhaps after a battle. I don't think anything needs to be done about that at the moment. If you feel there is an important interpretation issue, you should raise that with the service. Mr. Stamp, are you still questioning?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Yes, Your Honour. May I just have a moment to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have nothing further in re-examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Keric, you'll be pleased to know that that completes the questions for you. The Chamber has your evidence over yesterday and today, as well now it has the statement that you made originally in 2001 and the later one that you gave to Judge Dilparic, if we find that is confirmed. So we've got a great deal of material to consider. We are grateful for your attendance here and for the assistance that you've been able to provide. You may now return to your normal activities. You go with our thanks. The Court Officer will assist you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, I'm reminded that the statement to the Working Group, did you mean to tender that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think at this stage it should be received in evidence to provide a full context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01212.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That completes the evidence at this stage I think, Mr. Stamp. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, that completes the evidence we have available for this term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there any procedural matter you need to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It is something in line of a proposition, if I might take the liberty of doing that, Your Honours, and to give the Court information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber is not used to being propositioned, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Offer a suggestion, may I put it that way. Based on the remaining witnesses and the efforts we are making to get them, many of them are difficult to bring, we foresee that we would probably be closing the case some time around the first week of October. Having regard to the schedule as we know it in to the future. And it's really a matter for the Court. I was wondering if the Court might find it convenient just to indicate a provisional agenda or a provisional schedule as to how matters would stand in the -- thereafter. There would be perhaps a motion by the Defence, there would perhaps be issues as to the Defence case, and they might be given some time. I just suggest it because we are coming to the end of the year, and we have a lot of issues in respect to staffing and budgets that we probably would want to address depending on scheduling and timing and which might assist us. I just throw that one out. I also indicate that there may be two or three witnesses on the list that the Prosecution will indicate that it will not call to testify and will do so as a final decision is made during the recess. That is all I have to say, Your Honours. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Is there any particular procedural matter you would wish to raise at this stage, Mr. Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since the Trial Chamber doesn't often get propositioned to, I am not going to proposition to the Trial Chamber. I'm going to say there are no procedural matters to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I indicate, as this concludes the evidence available this week and we then go into court vacation, that the Chamber is increasingly conscious that we're coming toward the end of the list of Prosecution witnesses. We have concluded today the evidence of the 94th witness on the Prosecution list. We propose to resume again on Monday, the 17th of August. And in the three weeks following that, we will probably progress through the majority of the remaining witnesses, even though one or two of them can be expected to be longer than the average witness. It seemed to the Chamber that at that point, that is, after three more weeks of evidence, it would be convenient to give both parties an opportunity to reflect over their position, and in particular enable the Prosecution to determine which, if any, final witnesses they would intend to call. And both this period of the vacation and a period when we've heard three weeks more of witnesses in late August/the beginning of September would be an opportune time to enable the Defence to really finalise the thinking that has no doubt got under way at the present as to the course that their Defence might take once the Prosecution has finished its evidence. Therefore, the Chamber would not sit from Thursday, the -- or the 3rd of September until the week commencing Monday, the 21st of September. That is two weeks. Although, I think Monday, the 21st, is a United Nations holiday, so it would mean Tuesday the 22nd. But that would be for the purpose of enabling a final consideration by the Prosecution of whatever might then remain of its case and the Defence to consider in anticipation its position. The Defence at that point would need to consider whether or not a motion under 98 bis was contemplated, and failing that would need to be giving attention to its case outline, list of proposed witnesses and exhibits, and the steps that are required by the Rules before we'd commence hearing any Defence evidence that is intended to be called. In the Chamber's view, the three weeks of the vacation and those two additional weeks then in mid-September should very much enable both parties to be fairly clear about their position. The Chamber does not want at this point to press the Defence for any indication of its intentions, but what Mr. Stamp is hoping to glean is whether there can be some prediction of the length of time that might lie ahead after the close of the Prosecution case, how long the Defence would suggest it needs before commencing evidence, if that is the course taken, and roughly how long that evidence might take. Now, Mr. Djordjevic, if you want to give some general, non-binding indication of that, the Chamber would welcome it; but if they're matters you still have under consideration, we understand that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this moment, I am not able to provide you with any such indications; however, what the Trial Chamber may have noticed is very good cooperation between the Defence and the Prosecution when it comes to dealing with procedural matters outside of the courtroom. Whatever can be agreed between the two parties will be agreed in view of the expeditiousness of the trial. I would only ask my learned friend Stamp to inform us in due time what witnesses will be taken off the list because that may have an implication on the timing and also have consequences on the actions of the Defence. I expect, even without me saying this, that my learned friend Stamp will do his utmost to provide us with information in time and this will be beneficial both for the -- both parties and for the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Your position is understood, Mr. Djordjevic. Can the Chamber indicate then for the guidance of counsel on both sides that if there is to be a Rule 98 bis motion - we don't in any way suggest that there should be, but that's a matter for -- Defence decision - if there is to be a motion, the Chamber would expect that motion to be moved quickly at the end of the Prosecution case and would not be contemplating any adjournment to enable a long case to be prepared. And in the spirit of the new Rule of 98 bis, parties can expect the Chamber to deliver a decision orally as the Rule now contemplates within a day of the completion of the submissions on 98 bis. So there will not be any long delay if Rule 98 bis is pursued. If we are to proceed to Defence evidence, and that is subject to 98 bis and to the judgement of the Defence, we would also indicate that it is the Chamber's inclination to allow close to the minimum time, which are necessary for compliance with the Rules, from the end of the Prosecution case to the start of the Defence case. Certain documents have to be prepared and filed, but both Defence and Prosecuting counsel should expect that we would be looking in the order of two or three weeks at the most between the Prosecution case and the start of the Defence rather than any longer period that might commend itself to counsel. Now, of course if there is a particular issue or problem presented by that, the Chamber would expect to hear formal submission and reach a view. But our expectation is that we will move quickly and in the shortest time that is fair and reasonable from the Prosecution case to the hearing of any Defence case. Until we have some idea of the length, the number of witnesses, and the length of those, we cannot form any prediction, Mr. Stamp, as to the ultimate length of time that the trial will take. You will appreciate that. But you can expect a short period between close of Prosecution case and commencement of Defence case. I think that is all that we can usefully do at this stage to assist counsel in knowing what lies ahead as we're reaching the end of the Prosecution evidence. Our concern, as I have I think indicated before, is to try and ensure the completion of the evidence in this case in as short a time as can be done with fairness to both sides, and that will continue to be our objective. We wish you a profitable vacation, and we resume again in just over three weeks' time on Monday, the 17th of August. We now adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 17th day of August, 2009, at 2.15 p.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
